title: Grief
hookLine: Jesus wept; grief is love continuing

cards: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Martha says it on the road outside Bethany, the moment Jesus arrives. Her brother Lazarus has been in the tomb for days.
Later her sister Mary comes out, falls at his feet, and says the very same words. Two sisters, one sentence. If only you had been here.
Grieving people still say some version of it, to God, to a doctor, to themselves. And in John's telling, Jesus doesn't correct either of them.

teach.b: That sentence is half complaint, half trust: you could have stopped this, and you didn't come. John lets both sisters say it out loud, and nobody scolds them.

Martha keeps talking, and the two of them talk on the road about death and rising again. Grief, in this chapter, is allowed to speak. Then come the two words that make a whole verse in the King James Bible: Jesus wept.
When the mourners see it, they say, "Behold how he loved him!" Not how weak he is. How he loved him.
Some do ask why he couldn't have prevented the death, but the first thing John records is love. That's today's line: grief is love continuing after the person is gone.
Paul, writing to grieving Christians in Thessalonica, wants them to "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." He doesn't tell them not to sorrow.
He talks about how: with hope alongside. Some Christians hear that as comfort; some hear it, on hard days, as a weight. Both are honest.
And in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." The mourners are the ones named blessed.

Churches carry it differently: funerals and wakes, Orthodox memorial services with candles and a sweet dish of wheat, Catholics praying for the dead by name, Protestant families gathering for a meal after the burial.
Different customs, one instinct: grief deserves room.

how: Christians mourn through funerals, wakes and shared meals; Catholics pray and offer Masses for the dead, Orthodox Christians hold memorial services, and churches name the dead in prayer, holding sorrow and the hope of resurrection together.

o: the sorrow of loss, which the crowd read as love
a lack of hope that faith should overcome
a sadness meant to be over within a year

games.q: at the tomb of Lazarus — tap the pairs.
p: sorrow not, as those with no hope

both sisters say the very same sentence, and he doesn't correct either one.
Paul told grieving Christians not to sorrow at all

games.q: you're Martha. your brother has been in the tomb for days, and Jesus has only now arrived. what do you do?
o: stay in the house and say nothing.
go out to meet him and say it: if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
greet him politely and hide how you feel.
games.why: Martha goes out on the road and says it plainly, and later Mary says the same words. neither is scolded. grief is allowed to speak.

practice: Bring to mind someone or something you've lost, a person, a place, a version of your life, and let one memory come: their voice, a kitchen, a phrase they used.
If tears come, let them; if nothing comes, that's all right too; if you pray, tell God their name, and if you don't, hold the memory a little longer than you usually let yourself.
If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Grief. The sorrow of loss, which Jesus himself wept, and which the crowd at Lazarus's tomb read as love.

orig.note: Greek: he wept, shed tears. John 11:35 reads ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, Jesus wept.

carryVoice: Your line: grief is love. At Bethany, even the tears were read that way. Back tomorrow, same hill.
